HOW TO SUBMIT PUBLIC COMMENTS:
In Person:
Anyone who desires to address the City Council during
Open Forum
, must complete and file a pink speaker’s card with the City Clerk
prior
to the City Council’s consideration of the item.
Online speakers:
must raise their hand when instructed by the clerk. Once the City Clerk has announced the item and given a count of the number of total speakers, no person shall be permitted to speak on the item other than those persons who have submitted their names to the City Clerk or those that have their hand raised.
The amount of time allotted to individual speakers shall be determined based on the total number of persons requesting to speak during this item. The time allocation for each speaker will be as follows: 15 or fewer speakers, a maximum of 2 minutes; 16 to 24 speakers, a maximum of 1 and one-half minutes; and 25 or more speakers, a maximum of 1 minute.
NON-PUBLIC HEARING ITEMS LISTED ON THE AGENDA: Each speaker will be allowed up to TWO minutes to address the Council.  PUBLIC HEARING ITEMS: Speakers are allowed up to THREE (3) minutes to address the Council.
Via Zoom
:
Anyone who desires to address the City Council on items appearing on the agenda,
including Open Forum
, must raise their hand once public comment is open.
The public speakers attending in person will be called first, followed by Zoom participants (when appropriate).  Only those public speakers that have their hand raised at the appropriate time will be recognized.

Via mail:
received by 1:00 p.m. the day of the meeting, sent to 450 Civic Center Plaza, 3rd Floor, Office of the Clerk, Richmond, CA 94804.
Via eComments
: eComments are available once an agenda is published. Locate the meeting in "upcoming meetings" and click the comment bubble icon. Click on the item you wish to comment on. eComments can be submitted when the agenda is published and until the conclusion of public comments for the agenda item. Email your comment to
[email protected]
should you have difficulty submitting an eComment during a meeting.
Via email:
to
[email protected]
by 1:00 p.m
. the day of the meeting.
Emails
MUST
contain in the subject line 1) public comments – Open Session prior to Closed Session; 2) public comments – Open Forum; or 3) public comments agenda item #__ [include the agenda item number].
Properly labeled public comments
will be considered a public record, put into the official meeting record, available after the meeting as supplemental materials, and will be posted as an attachment to the meeting minutes when the minutes are posted:
http://www.ci.richmond.ca.us/Archive.aspx?AMID=31
The City cannot guarantee that its network and/or the site will be uninterrupted. To ensure that the City Council receives your comments, you are strongly encouraged to submit your comments in writing in advance of the meeting.
Procedures for Removing Items from the Consent Calendar
:
Members of the public who request to remove an item from the consent calendar must first discuss the item with a staff member by phone or a back-and-forth email discussion, and state the name of the staff member when requesting removal of the item from the consent calendar
(by 2 p.m. the day of the meeting)
.  The procedures for discussion do not apply to items sponsored by the mayor or councilmembers.
Any member of the City Council who would like to remove an item from the consent calendar must notify the appropriate staff person and the City Clerk’s Office prior to the meeting. Although members of the City Council are encouraged to ask questions and share concerns with staff ahead of the meeting, they are not required to do so.
The Clerk’s Office must be informed of any requests to remove items from the Consent Calendar. Items removed from the Consent Calendar shall be placed at the end of the agenda for consideration.
CONDUCT AT MEETINGS:
Richmond City Council meetings are limited public forums during which the City strives to provide an open, safe atmosphere and promote robust public debate. Members of the public, however, must comply with state law, as well as the City’s laws and procedures and may not actually disrupt the orderly conduct of these meetings. The public, for example, may not shout or use amplifying devices, must submit comment cards and speak during their allotted time, may not create a physical disturbance, may not speak on matters unrelated to issues within the jurisdiction of the City Council or the agenda item at hand, and may not cause immediate threats to public safety.
Click here for City Harassment Policy
Accessibility for Individuals with Disabilities:
Upon request, the City will provide for written agenda materials in appropriate alternative formats, or disability-related modification or accommodation, including auxiliary aids or services and sign language interpreters, to enable individuals with disabilities to participate in and provide comments at/related to public meetings. Please submit a request, including your name, phone number and/or email address, and a description of the modification, accommodation, auxiliary aid, service or alternative format requested at least two days before the meeting.  Requests should be emailed to
[email protected]
or submitted by phone at 510-620-6513, ext. 9, or 510-620-6509.  Requests made by mail to City Clerk’s Office, City Council meeting, 450 Civic Center Plaza, Richmond, CA 94804 must be received at least two days before the meeting. Requests will be granted whenever possible and resolved in favor of accessibility.
Unless otherwise noted in an agenda description, all actions taken by the Council include a determination that CEQA does not apply (i.e., the action is not a project and therefore exempt from CEQA).
Disclaimer:  The City Clerk's Office translates agendas to enhance public access.  Translated agendas are provided as a courtesy and do not constitute legal notice of the meeting or items to be discussed.  In case of discrepancy, the English agenda will prevail.

Devin W.
I'm in support of continued use of ALPR technology and switching to Axon from Flock.

This isn't theoretical. Just last month in El Cerrito, after that city removed its own license plate cameras, police said the loss of that data slowed the investigation into the murder of 21-year-old Jakai Couch. It was fixed and ALPR cameras in Richmond that ultimately helped identify the suspects' vehicle and led to two arrests so far.

Here in Richmond, fixed and ALPR cameras also helped identify the suspect in the fatal hit-and-run that killed 81-year-old Rafael Gutierrez Delgado last month.

These aren't abstract benefits. These cases have suspects in custody and their families have timely answers they might not have gotten otherwise, if ever.

As with any surveillance technology, I support ALPR with appropriate guardrails including 30-day retention limits, regular audits, clear policies on who can query the data and why, and meaningful oversight and accountability when something goes wrong.

I also prefer Richmond owning the cameras vs. leasing them, and having the data stored with evidence.com.

Richmond has actually led the Bay Area on this front. As far as I'm aware, we're the only city in the region operating a closed ALPR system, meaning our data isn't shared out to other agencies by default or choice in California (and nationally). That's the best model, so don't abandon it.
Edith Alderette
I've watched this topic for years, and until recently, I was agnostic. I see both the pros and cons of the ALPR systems. Recent events, particularly the recent El Cerrito murder and the hit-and-run homicide on 23rd St. where cameras were key to apprehending the suspects, have changed my mind. ALPRs have saved numerous people, apprehending in minutes suspects in murders and child abductions that otherwise may have taken hours, days, or weeks; time that would allow the criminals to do even more harm. The key is these systems need to be used RESPONSIBLY, and I believe RPD will do just that. I venture to guess that opponents so dead set against ALPRs would be all for them had their child was abducted, assaulted, or murdered and police are unable to do anything because they have no leads. The alternative is a residential dragnet, which is even more invasive. How many more major crimes in Richmond must go unsolved before we can accept that this is the best solution available to us? And it's not as if these systems are permanent; if and when better technology exists, we can remove them. These are the tools we have now, and we need them. We can't rail against the ineffectiveness of the RPD to prevent and solve crimes when we don't give them the tools they need to do their jobs. I implore you to approve Axon and the ALPRs in Richmond. If they don't work, we'll know soon enough and can remove them, but I have a feeling that it will only take a few major crimes solved quickly to have opponents change their minds.
cecil calban
Nothing is perfect, including privacy, concerns surrounding safety cameras.

Nevertheless, I support these, and we have already seen how many crimes they have helped solve, including a recent murder and a recent hit and run death.

Our police department is under staff and under constant bombardment by certain council members and political groups, claiming to be grassroots, who are anti-Police and have records of being so.

Our police department is decimated, so we call the city Council to give them any help in solving crimes without weapons.
Philip Rosenthal
Recently, ALPRS were used Help solve a murder of  a black man on  our border with El Cerrito. APLRS cameras were also used to help solve the  hit-and-run murder Latino man on 23rd St.


Council members are constantly demanding that the police department use passive, non-lethal or less lethal policing methods.

This is one of them. I acknowledge the privacy concerns, but if that’s the case, the city should immediately resend CCTV cameras on all  city property and staff  should  be forced to  use telephones without the ability to record.

There are thousands of cameras in Richmond, but we don’t have or any detectives to sort through this.

Recently, in our neighborhood, two thieves attacked children in their own driveway.

Police detectives were desperately trying to find video, but the only video available that would’ve shown the escaping car belonged to a private business who did not release it.

Everything is imperfect, including the ALPRS system. But that doesn’t mean that the criminals take priority over the taxpayers.
Meagan Travlos
Big brother surveillance keeps no one safe. The amount of money being used and proposed to spy on residents is astounding. ALPRs do not decrease crime and can in fact leave our city open to major security risks through hacking. They are overwhelming used in Black and Brown communities, furthering a history of oppression. I am against all ALPR systems in Richmond.
Ben S.
All ALPR systems should be suspended in the city of Richmond, this is a violation of privacy that is ineffective. And the data shows it. The crime rate in the 11 months prior to the flock suspension, during 3 month flock suspension, and after flock reinstatement are exactly the same!
Alicia Alexander
Axon is just a different company offering the same so called services as Flock.  Axon has proven to be just as problematic with its lack of security and abuse by those with access to the cameras and databases - numerous cases of law enforcement officers using it to stalk women and intimate partners. Axon and Flock have also been weaponized against women seeking shelter from domestic violence & abortion / reproductive healthcare. Axon is also used in partnership with ICE/DHS.  Richmond is a sanctuary city per Ordinances 29-90, 12-18, as well as the update on 3/25/2025 as such should not support anything that enables ICE in our community.   Save the money and invest in community based policing that is proven to work instead to supporting violations of the 4th amendment and warrantless surveillance violating peoples expectation of privacy even in public spaces.  We don't need a surveillance state - we need trust built through relationships and social supports that end crime in our community.

agenda_briefs.title: Council to vote on awarding Basin 4 lease to STAX Engineering
agenda_briefs.summary: Council will consider awarding STAX Engineering a lease for Basin 4 at the Point Potrero Marine Terminal as a maritime emissions control hub and Northern California headquarters. Base rent is $210,000 annually ($17,500/month) for an initial five-year term with two five-year extension options (15 years total). STAX plans about $525,000 in improvements over the first five years and expects roughly 125 permanent maritime and technical jobs. The current tenant's lease expires October 2026; commencement is anticipated in or after November 2026.

Devin W.
I'm in support of continued use of ALPR technology and switching to Axon from Flock.

This isn't theoretical. Just last month in El Cerrito, after that city removed its own license plate cameras, police said the loss of that data slowed the investigation into the murder of 21-year-old Jakai Couch. It was fixed and ALPR cameras in Richmond that ultimately helped identify the suspects' vehicle and led to two arrests so far.

Here in Richmond, fixed and ALPR cameras also helped identify the suspect in the fatal hit-and-run that killed 81-year-old Rafael Gutierrez Delgado last month.

These aren't abstract benefits. These cases have suspects in custody and their families have timely answers they might not have gotten otherwise, if ever.

As with any surveillance technology, I support ALPR with appropriate guardrails including 30-day retention limits, regular audits, clear policies on who can query the data and why, and meaningful oversight and accountability when something goes wrong.

I also prefer Richmond owning the cameras vs. leasing them, and having the data stored with evidence.com.

Richmond has actually led the Bay Area on this front. As far as I'm aware, we're the only city in the region operating a closed ALPR system, meaning our data isn't shared out to other agencies by default or choice in California (and nationally). That's the best model, so don't abandon it.
Edith Alderette
I've watched this topic for years, and until recently, I was agnostic. I see both the pros and cons of the ALPR systems. Recent events, particularly the recent El Cerrito murder and the hit-and-run homicide on 23rd St. where cameras were key to apprehending the suspects, have changed my mind. ALPRs have saved numerous people, apprehending in minutes suspects in murders and child abductions that otherwise may have taken hours, days, or weeks; time that would allow the criminals to do even more harm. The key is these systems need to be used RESPONSIBLY, and I believe RPD will do just that. I venture to guess that opponents so dead set against ALPRs would be all for them had their child was abducted, assaulted, or murdered and police are unable to do anything because they have no leads. The alternative is a residential dragnet, which is even more invasive. How many more major crimes in Richmond must go unsolved before we can accept that this is the best solution available to us? And it's not as if these systems are permanent; if and when better technology exists, we can remove them. These are the tools we have now, and we need them. We can't rail against the ineffectiveness of the RPD to prevent and solve crimes when we don't give them the tools they need to do their jobs. I implore you to approve Axon and the ALPRs in Richmond. If they don't work, we'll know soon enough and can remove them, but I have a feeling that it will only take a few major crimes solved quickly to have opponents change their minds.
cecil calban
Nothing is perfect, including privacy, concerns surrounding safety cameras.

Nevertheless, I support these, and we have already seen how many crimes they have helped solve, including a recent murder and a recent hit and run death.

Our police department is under staff and under constant bombardment by certain council members and political groups, claiming to be grassroots, who are anti-Police and have records of being so.

Our police department is decimated, so we call the city Council to give them any help in solving crimes without weapons.
Philip Rosenthal
Recently, ALPRS were used Help solve a murder of  a black man on  our border with El Cerrito. APLRS cameras were also used to help solve the  hit-and-run murder Latino man on 23rd St.


Council members are constantly demanding that the police department use passive, non-lethal or less lethal policing methods.

This is one of them. I acknowledge the privacy concerns, but if that’s the case, the city should immediately resend CCTV cameras on all  city property and staff  should  be forced to  use telephones without the ability to record.

There are thousands of cameras in Richmond, but we don’t have or any detectives to sort through this.

Recently, in our neighborhood, two thieves attacked children in their own driveway.

Police detectives were desperately trying to find video, but the only video available that would’ve shown the escaping car belonged to a private business who did not release it.

Everything is imperfect, including the ALPRS system. But that doesn’t mean that the criminals take priority over the taxpayers.
Meagan Travlos
Big brother surveillance keeps no one safe. The amount of money being used and proposed to spy on residents is astounding. ALPRs do not decrease crime and can in fact leave our city open to major security risks through hacking. They are overwhelming used in Black and Brown communities, furthering a history of oppression. I am against all ALPR systems in Richmond.
Ben S.
All ALPR systems should be suspended in the city of Richmond, this is a violation of privacy that is ineffective. And the data shows it. The crime rate in the 11 months prior to the flock suspension, during 3 month flock suspension, and after flock reinstatement are exactly the same!
Alicia Alexander

agenda_briefs.title: Council to consider LPR effectiveness study and EFF presentation
agenda_briefs.summary: Richmond Council will consider directing staff to arrange a presentation by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) at a future council meeting on the effectiveness, limitations, and impacts of license plate reader (LPR) cameras. Staff would also be asked to bring objective statistical analysis of Richmond data on whether LPRs reduce crime, recover stolen vehicles, support investigations, and lead to arrests and convictions, plus information on data retention and information sharing for any LPR systems under consideration. The item has no financial impact and no decision has been made yet.

agenda_briefs.title: Council to consider Keller Beach sewer study and next steps
agenda_briefs.summary: Council will receive a presentation on the draft Keller Beach Sanitary Sewer (KBSS) Feasibility Study, which looks at the current state of the sewer system and possible fixes. Council is set to give staff direction on which interim (short-term) and long-term improvements to move forward with. Staff would then return with a final report and recommended action in November or December 2026. No decisions have been made yet.
agenda_briefs.action_required: Watch for the November/December 2026 final report — this could affect sewer service and costs in the Keller Beach area.
